I’ve been struggling for about nine months now—things started subtly but just kept getting worse. For the past seven months, I’ve felt this heaviness, like I’m moving through mud. I don’t enjoy my job anymore, and I barely have the energy to get out of bed, even after eight hours of sleep. My wife says I’ve been slow—like when I pick up my coffee or reach for my keys, I just… drag.  

But it’s not just the sadness. For the last six months, I’ve been certain something’s terribly wrong inside me—like my organs are rotting or shrinking. The doctors can’t find anything, but I *feel* it. And sometimes, I swear I feel bugs crawling under my skin, especially at night. No one else does. I’ve tried to explain it, but the words come out tangled—like “spoon, moon, swoon,” just because they sound alike. I know it doesn’t make sense, but I can’t stop it.  

Work’s a mess—I can’t focus, and my team noticed. I lost the drive to do anything meaningful. The truth is, I used to be in control. Now, I don’t recognize myself.

I can’t focus—my thoughts slip into words that only make sense to me, like “*glarnix*” for when the silence between notes speaks louder than music.

I used to love tattooing, the buzz of the needle, the clients telling me how it changed something in them. But now? I can’t even sit still long enough to line up a stencil. I pace in the back, picking at my cuticles until they bleed. Doesn’t matter—nobody’s coming anyway. The world’s ending, you know? Not in some movie way. Quiet. Like we’re all just fading into static.  

Sometimes I taste metal—like sucking on a battery—outta nowhere. No food, nothing. Just… copper and rot. Doctors say it’s not real, but I *feel* it. And people? They don’t get it. I stopped going out. My friends stopped calling. Easier this way. I say stupid things sometimes—start laughing for no reason, act like a kid. It’s embarrassing, but it just… happens.  

I don’t care about anything anymore. Not the shop, not my apartment, not even eating. Some days I think, “Just don’t wake up. That’d be fine.” I’m no good to anyone. Never was.  

The strange stuff—tastes, thoughts, the way my words jump around when I talk—it’s been like this seven months, even when I’m not feeling low. But mostly, I’m just… empty. Like the light’s out.

I used to lose myself in designing pieces, but now I can’t even bring myself to open my tool drawer. I move so slow; just getting out of my chair to answer the door feels like I’m underwater.  

People say things, and I know they’re talking about me—like when my assistant mentioned “adjusting settings” on a ring, and I *felt* it—the vibrations under my skin, like tiny hands crawling over my arms. It’s always there, even when I’m alone. Once, a client glanced at her watch, and I *knew* she was signaling someone—sending a message about me. I had to leave the room.  

I don’t see friends. What’s the point? I’m a burden—broken. Some days I think, “Wouldn’t it be easier if I just didn’t wake up?” I’m not going to hurt myself, but… I wouldn’t mind disappearing.  

My thoughts get tangled. I’ll start talking about a pendant design and end up on the weather in Alaska—my assistant just stares. And sometimes I make faces I don’t mean to—like my face doesn’t belong to me.  

There were weeks I didn’t leave bed… but even when I felt a bit better, those voices, the crawling—they stayed. They don’t need my sadness to exist.

I’ve been struggling for about a year now, maybe a little longer. It started around the same time I stopped enjoying teaching—the kids used to make me smile, but now I can barely find the energy to get out of bed in the morning. I keep replaying moments from the past—things I said that might’ve hurt someone, even if they didn’t notice. I’ll stand by the classroom window and suddenly get this overwhelming urge to step off the ledge, even though I know I wouldn’t do it.  

But it’s not just sadness. There’s more. I can taste something in my mouth all the time—like rust and salt, even when I haven’t eaten. Doctors find nothing. I worry the water system’s poisoned, and soon everyone will collapse. The world feels like it’s collapsing already, like it’s already gone. I call it “the hush”—that’s when everything stops, and I know the end’s here. I don’t plan anything anymore; even showering takes too much effort. And sometimes, without realizing, I catch myself copying the kids—mirroring their hand motions or facial expressions.  

For seven months, it’s been like this—this heavy gray dragging with me, wrapped in fear.
